word_order: SVO | Subjects precede verbs and then objects in examples like 'Steve Jobs unveiled the device' and 'Mutations can have a variety of different effects.'
register: edited written expository prose (news / encyclopedic / technical), formal and non-spontaneous
clause_boundary_signals: relative pronouns introducing subordinate clauses (who, that)
subordinating conjunctions that introduce dependent clauses (although, because)
coordinating conjunctions that join independent clauses (and)
reduced participial clauses that attach as separate propositions (causing, leaving)
non_boundary_traps: sentence-initial prepositional/temporal adjuncts that look like full clauses (For over a thousand years, Around 60 cases)
numerical/quantifier noun-phrases that fill the left periphery but are not complete clauses (Eighteen percent, Around 60 cases)
appositive or title-bearing noun phrases that contain internal structure (Sir Richard Branson's Virgin Group)
reduced participial/nominal phrases that resemble clauses but function as modifiers (going across the sky, emitting photons)
unstable_prefix_signals: initial nominal/quantifier phrases (Eighteen percent...) where continuation may decide predicate scope
sentence-initial prepositional/temporal phrases (For over a thousand years...) whose attachment is still unresolved
contrastive subordinators that can serve multiple discourse roles (while, although)
notes_for_prompt_writer: The source uses English SVO order with frequent subordination and coordination; clauses are often linked by subordinators and relative pronouns. Sentence-initial adjuncts (temporal/prepositional) and numeral/quantifier noun-phrases commonly occupy the left periphery and can be structurally ambiguous. Reduced participial clauses and appositive noun phrases appear regularly and should be treated as clause-like material in the source.
